title: Small molecules targeting SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid reveal a conserved RNA-binding vulnerability across human coronaviruses.
abstract: SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 exemplify the persistent threat posed by coronaviruses, with their capacity for zoonotic spill over, rapid transmission, and severe disease resulting in substantial morbidity, mortality, and socio-economic burden. The repeated emergence of highly pathogenic coronaviruses highlights the urgent need for broad-spectrum therapeutic strategies. The nucleocapsid (N) protein, essential for RNA binding, genome packaging, and viral replication, remains a highly conserved yet underexplored antiviral target. Sequence alignment revealed 90% identity between SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV N proteins, and 48.1% identity between SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV N proteins. In our earlier work, we identified two small molecules, ceftazidime and sennoside A, that bind the N-terminal domain of the SARS-CoV-2 N protein and inhibit nucleic acid binding, and identified their binding sites using NMR chemical shift perturbation assays. Here, we observed that several residues involved in inhibitor binding are conserved across betacoronaviruses, suggesting a shared druggable vulnerability. We have purified recombinant N proteins from SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2, and demonstrated by electrophoretic mobility shift assays that both compounds significantly reduced RNA binding. Their inhibitory concentrations (IC50) were determined using fluorescence polarization. The docking analyses indicated that both inhibitors target the RNA-binding pocket of the N-NTD, consistent with a conserved mechanism of action. Collectively, our findings reveal a conserved RNA-binding vulnerability in coronavirus N proteins and highlights the pan-coronavirus therapeutic potential of these inhibitors.

title: Optimal compositions of potent sliced-siRNA with DNA bases substitution and insights of Ago2 slicing actions
abstract: We have previously characterized the nucleotide compositions of single-stranded ago2-sliced small interfering RNAs (sliced-siRNA, sliRNA), a novel type of potent RNAi trigger designed based on the biogenesis mechanism of miRNA-451. sliRNAs have on par antisense mediated silencing activity but about 1000-fold reduced passenger strand activity compared to siRNA. In the current study, to further characterize sliRNAs to facilitate their in vivo application, we have investigated the effects of substituting RNA nucleotides (nts) in sliRNA with DNA nts (sliDRNAs), which will allow us to study the potential effects on their processing, maturation, and silencing activity from individual or multiple nts at different positions. Our results showed sliDRNAs have distinguished composition from siRNA with DNA nts (siDRNA), indicated that, in addition to their different biogenesis mechanisms, these two types of RNAi triggers may also have adopted additional different silencing mechanisms. Our results also revealed some mechanism related to how Ago2 executes its slicer activity and the effects on sliRNA potency by trimming and tailing during sliRNA maturation. These results have paved the way for using other chemically modified nts in sliRNAs that may enhance their in vivo stability and transportability to facilitate their in vivo applications.

title: Differential transcriptional and translational responses of aryl hydrocarbon receptor and biotransformation enzymes to environmentally relevant polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon mixtures in hen ovarian follicles.
abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are environmental contaminants that may disrupt ovarian function. Because organisms are exposed to complex xenobiotic mixtures, this study examined the effects of two PAH mixtures, MIX I and MIX II, representing concentrations determined in eggs from free-range and caged hens, respectively, on biotransformation-related factors in the hen ovary. Laying hens were exposed to these mixtures for 7 or 28 days, and small and large white prehierarchical follicles (SWFs and LWFs, respectively), along with the granulosa and theca layers of the three largest preovulatory follicles (F3-F1), were analysed for AhR, CYP1B1, COMT, and GST messenger RNA (mRNA) and protein expression. Exposure to the mixtures did not affect mRNA expression in prehierarchical follicles. After 7 days, CYP1B1 showed the strongest transcriptional response, with marked induction in the granulosa layer and moderate changes in the theca layer of F3-F1 follicles, mainly after exposure to MIX I. After 28 days, there were no changes in mRNA expression. In contrast, there were more extensive changes in protein abundance after prolonged exposure. Short-term exposure reduced AhR protein in SWFs after exposure to MIX I and GST in LWFs after exposure to MIX II. MIX II decreased CYP1B1 protein in the granulosa layer of F2 follicles, whereas COMT and GST protein abundance declined in the theca layer of F3 and F1 follicles. After 28 days, both mixtures reduced CYP1B1 protein in SWFs and in the granulosa layer of F3 follicles, while MIX II also reduced CYP1B1 in LWFs and the F1 granulosa layer, and reduced AhR, COMT, and GST in the theca layer of all preovulatory follicles. In conclusion, PAH mixtures affected biotransformation pathways in the hen ovary depending on the tissue, follicle size, exposure duration, and the type of mixture administered (MIX I or MIX II), with prolonged exposure reflected at the protein level.

title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa MucP limits RNA phage propagation by targeting phage lysis.
abstract: Lytic phages culminate their lifecycle by causing lysis of the infected host cell. Although the molecular basis of phage-mediated lysis has been studied extensively, bacterial mechanisms that interfere with the lysis stage remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that MucP, a site 2 protease of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA), mitigates the activity of the RNA phage PP7 lysis protein (LP), which contains a transmembrane (TM) helix, suggesting that MucP is a bacterial factor compromising PP7-induced lysis. We identified an LP variant (LP*) having enhanced helical propensity by P26L and S40L mutations, which was refractory to MucP and exhibited killing activity against PA strains that are resistant to the wild-type LP, revealing an inverse correlation between MucP activity and LP susceptibility. A PP7 mutant carrying LP* exhibited MucP-escaper phenotype, forming discernible plaques regardless of MucP overexpression, albeit with a fitness cost reflected in reduced phage progeny production. Collectively, these findings suggest that MucP targets the TM helix of the PP7 LP, providing a function compromising phage lysis by repurposing a host-encoded protease in PA.

title: Identification of T-Cell specific signature miRNAs and target pathways in Psoriasis
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation, involving T cells as the major players in the manifestation of lesional and systemic inflammation. With the extensive exploration of keratinocyte dysfunctionality, T cell centric deregulation has gained much focus with limited molecular understanding in the context of disease etiology. miRNAs, the molecular switches known to drive disease manifestation via altering keratinocyte biology, have not been much studied in the context of T cell alterations. This study aims to explore T cell-associated miRNAs and their target signaling networks to understand their role in modulating psoriasis specific T cell changes. miRNAs with altered expression in psoriatic T cells were identified through a comprehensive analysis of the available literature and datasets. The relevant miRNAs were used for prediction and enrichment of cognate targets and mapping of associated pathways involved in different modalities of T cell functionality. The study identified 14 miRNAs dysregulated in psoriatic T cells along with 256 downstream targets involved in 15 distinct T cell associated signaling pathways. 5/14 miRNAs identified were further validated with a significant increase in their expression in enriched CD3+T cells from blood of psoriatic patients versus healthy subjects. The psoriatic T cell specific miRNA driven signaling cascades identified were modelled to propose yet unexplored molecular basis of dysregulated T cell activation, proliferation, survival, and subset differentiation associated with the disease. The new findings delineate candidate miRNA target signaling components that need to be validated in T cell disease etiology. Importantly, the key miRNAs/targets can be employed towards psoriasis-specific diagnostics and therapeutic interventions.

title: Cornified envelope-related gene expression is epigenetically regulated by TET in basal keratinocytes of epidermis.
abstract: The epidermis comprises multiple cell populations derived from basal keratinocyte differentiation. Although keratinization is tightly regulated, its molecular mechanisms remain unclear, specifically with regard to epigenetic regulation, including DNA demethylation. This study aimed to elucidate the mechanisms of epidermal keratinization, focusing on ten-eleven translocation (TET)-dependent changes in DNA hydroxymethylation in basal keratinocytes. Newborn rat epidermal keratinocytes that undergo keratinization during culture were treated with Tet2/3-targeting small interfering RNA and vitamin C (VC), a cofactor for TET activity. Global 5-methylcytosine and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) levels were quantified using dot blot analysis. DNA microarray and RT-qPCR analyses were performed to identify the genes regulated by TET. Protein expression alterations during keratinization were analyzed using western blotting. VC significantly increased 5-hmC levels, whereas no statistically significant increase was observed under Tet2/3 knockdown. Gene Ontology analysis identified cornified envelope (CE) as an enriched term among genes downregulated by Tet2/3 knockdown. VC enhanced the expression of CE-related genes (filaggrin, trichohyalin, loricrin, and cornifelin) at later stages of keratinization, accompanied by increased protein levels. These findings suggest an association between TET-dependent changes in 5-hmC and CE-related gene expression during keratinocyte differentiation.

title: Pathological Ossification of Spinal Ligament-Derived Fibroblasts in an Inflammatory Micro-Environment via Activation of the ECM/ITGA5/FAK/AKT Pathway in Ankylosing Spondylitis.
abstract: Chronic inflammation and heterotopic ossification (HO) were typical hallmarks of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). Although existing target inflammation inhibitors could reduce inflammation but failed to halt HO progression, highlighting the need for osteogenesis-specific treatments. However, the role of fibroblasts (Fbs) responsible for extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling in AS-associated pathological ossification remained unclear. In this study, osteogenic capacity, pathological condition and underlying molecular pathways for Fbs derived from AS spinal ligaments were validated. Fbs from uncalcified spinal ligaments of age-matched AS patients/controls were compared. AS-Fbs were treated with a gradient concentration of TNF-α during osteogenic induction. Meanwhile, specific inhibition of AKT phosphorylation was applied to confirm the role of PI3K/AKT in osteogenesis. Upstream signalling pathways were also explored via RNA-sequencing. Additionally, in vivo, subcutaneous cell transplantation was performed to simulate ectopic ossification. AS-Fbs possessed superior osteogenic capacity than controls. Moreover, osteogenic signs could be promoted by low concentration TNF-α-induced inflammatory micro-environment. Functional analysis revealed a crucial role of the PI3K/AKT pathway. Mechanistically, RNA-seq identified the ECM/integrin subunit alpha 5 (ITGA5)/focal adhesion kinase (FAK) upstream pathway. In detail, osteogenic induction increased ECM protein levels including thrombospondin-1 (THBS1) and fibulin-1 (FBLN1), activating ITGA5, subsequent FAK phosphorylation, osteogenic markers expression and eventually inducing Fb-to-osteocyte differentiation. ITGA5 knockdown or specific FAK inhibition attenuated osteogenic phenotypes and reduced osteogenic proteins expression. Regarding in vivo experiments, subcutaneous bone-like tissue formation derived from transplantation of AS-Fbs was identified and could be suppressed significantly via the AKT phosphorylation inhibition. In conclusion, the findings of this study revealed potential causes for HO progression derived from AS-Fbs in spite of effective anti-inflammation therapy. Furthermore, the crucial role of ECM/ITGA5/FAK/AKT axial signalling pathways in the aberrant osteogenesis of AS-Fbs was identified. Combined targeted intervention at the aforementioned signals and application of anti-inflammatory agents might be a novel potential strategy for the treatment of pathological ectopic ossification caused by AS.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering.
abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor-encapsulated within a GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle-leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

title: ACTR5 as a potential therapeutic target in AML: Preliminary mechanistic insights from integrated multi-omics analysis.
abstract: Actin-Related Protein 5(ACTR5) is essential for tumor progression in hepatocellular carcinoma(HCC), however, its function in acute myeloid leukemia(AML) remains elusive. We aim to characterize the role of ACTR5 in AML progression as well as its potential mechanism. The patient samples from TCGA and GTEx database were utilized to reveal the survival of ACTR5 high-expression(ACTR5hi) and low-expression(ACTR5low) through GEPIA online tool. ACTR5 knockout (ACTR5-KO) cell lines were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology and ACTR5 overexpression(ACTR5-OE) cell line was obtained by plenti-CMV transfection system, to assess its impact on cell growth, apoptosis and cell cycle in vitro. Functionally essential targets were revealed via integrative analysis of multi-omics data, including RNA-seq and ATAC-seq, between wild-type and ACTR5-KO cell lines. The ACTR5hi patients showed a shorter overall survival compared to the ACTR5low patients in AML group. Besides, ACTR5 depletion inhibited proliferation, promoted apoptosis, and impaired cell cycle progression. Mechanistic studies unveiled ACTR5 as a regulator of cell cycle, including abnormal expression of checkpoints promoting G1/S phase transition(CCND2)and inhibiting S/G2 phase transition(FOS, JUNB). In addition, the functionally essential genes of DNA repair were revealed including the upregulation of RAD50, ATM, CDC20, CDC25C, TERT. Our findings highlight the potential oncogenic role of ACTR5 in poor prognosis, as well as suggesting a potential role for ACTR5 in AML pathogenesis through its association with disrupted cell cycle and DNA repair gene programs.

title: Direction-aware multi-cohort integration reveals biologically coherent but directionally discordant peripheral-blood transcriptomic signatures in major depressive disorder.
abstract: Peripheral-blood transcriptomic studies of major depressive disorder (MDD) frequently identify biologically coherent signals but show limited cross-cohort reproducibility. The study applied a direction-aware, multi-cohort framework that distinguished discovery, internal prediction, external association, directional replication and matched cross-omic support. Discovery analyses were conducted in GSE255685, comprising 180 participants with MDD and 99 controls. Differential-expression, functional-enrichment, protein-protein interaction and leakage-controlled machine-learning analyses identified 375 differentially expressed genes, including 112 with higher and 263 with lower expression in MDD. Convergent analyses implicated three principal biological components involving ribosome-associated translation, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, and chemokine-linked inflammatory or immediate-early stress signalling. Integration of 11 predictive, explainability and network-topology rankings using a rule-based support criterion yielded an exploratory 18-gene discovery-prioritization family. In a held-out test set of 56 participants, logistic-regression and support-vector-machine models each achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.999 and an accuracy of 98.2%, indicating strong within-cohort discrimination but not external clinical validation. External RNA assessment in GSE251778 identified significant candidate-family associations for TRIM56, PPP1R15A, DDIT3 and NFKBIA; however, all four effects were opposite to those observed in discovery, and 15 of 18 genes had opposite-direction estimates across cohorts. Thus, no gene met the prespecified criterion for strict same-direction replication. Among 146 participants with matched RNA, microRNA and DNA-methylation data, 241 microRNA-mRNA associations remained FDR-significant, including 36 directionally coherent inverse pairs involving 10 genes. Five CpG-mRNA associations were significant despite the absence of targeted differential methylation. No candidate-gene stress-response contrast survived multiple-testing correction. These findings show that pathway-level coherence and strong internal classification do not necessarily translate into portable gene-level biomarkers. Direction-aware integration may therefore be essential for distinguishing reproducible molecular features from cohort-dependent peripheral-blood expression states in MDD.

title: Multi-omics integration identifies core genes, molecular subtypes, and IDI1-centered immune microenvironment mechanisms in coronary artery disease.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. We integrated transcriptomic datasets (GSE113079, GSE98583, GSE71226) and single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE159677) from GEO. Differential expression analysis, WGCNA, machine learning, molecular clustering, immune infiltration analysis, CellChat, in silico knockout, and PheWAS were applied to investigate CAD-related molecular networks. We identified 99 DEGs and the MEturquoise module as a CAD-associated module. Machine learning initially identified four candidate genes (RC3H1, IDI1, RAB2A, and SIRPB2); however, only IDI1 was retained after external validation and single-cell intersection. Single-cell analysis revealed macrophage expansion and specific IDI1 enrichment in Cycling cells and immune populations. CAD was classified into two molecular subtypes with distinct immune profiles. Cell communication analysis identified SPP1, TNF, CCL, and MIF pathways as key inflammatory regulators. Virtual knockout simulation of IDI1 affected hemostasis, Toll-like receptor signaling, and collagen degradation pathways. PheWAS showed no significant phenotype-wide associations for IDI1. This study identified IDI1 as a CAD-associated candidate gene, revealed immune-based molecular subtypes of CAD, and suggested that IDI1 and inflammatory signaling pathways may serve as potential therapeutic targets, providing insights into precision classification and targeted therapy for CAD.

title: Resolving melanoma heterogeneity at single-cell resolution: implications for target discovery and therapy resistance.
abstract: Melanoma is characterized by profound intra-tumoural heterogeneity and a complex tumour microenvironment (TME), which are primary drivers of therapy resistance. Conventional bulk sequencing lacks the resolution to capture these cellular nuances. Single-cell technologies, particularly single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial multiomics, have fundamentally advanced our understanding of melanoma by enabling high-resolution characterization of malignant cell states, immune ecosystems and tumour microenvironment interactions. In this review, we summarize recent advances in single-cell multiomics studies of melanoma heterogeneity and therapy resistance, focusing on the identification of drug-tolerant persister states, immune escape mechanisms and resistance-associated cellular transitions. We further discuss how single-cell approaches facilitate target discovery, biomarker development and the rational design of combination therapies. By integrating multiomics profiling, computational modelling and pharmacological validation, these technologies provide a framework for translating cellular-level insights into precision therapeutic strategies. Finally, we highlight current challenges and future opportunities for clinical implementation of single-cell-guided approaches in refractory melanoma.

title: Identification and validation of circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers for endometriosis through integrating machine learning and single-cell analysis.
abstract: Endometriosis (EMs) is a chronic inflammatory disease, and the lack of candidate molecular biomarkers remain a major clinical challenge. Circadian rhythm disruption plays a non-negligible role in EMs. However, the diagnostic potential of circadian rhythm-related biomarkers remains insufficiently validated. We performed weighted gene co-expression network analysis to screen for endometriosis-related hub modules. Four machine learning algorithms were used for feature selection in the training cohort, and the resulting diagnostic model was evaluated in three independent GEO validation cohorts. To evaluate the immune microenvironment, we applied MCPcounter, CIBERSORT, and single-sample gene set enrichment analysis. Single‑cell RNA‑seq data were processed with Seurat for cell clustering and annotation, cell‑cell communication networks were constructed using CellChat, and pseudotime trajectory analysis was performed with Monocle. SMC2, SUV39H2, and TIMELESS were identified as candidate molecular biomarkers, demonstrating favorable diagnostic performance across three independent validation sets. Computational immune infiltration analysis suggested higher enrichment scores for B cells and CD8+ T cells, along with lower scores for Tregs and NK cells in EMs samples. Single-cell analysis revealed an increased proportion of mesenchymal cells in EMs samples and altered cell-cell communication involving BMP, CHEMERIN, and GRN signaling pathways. Pseudotime analysis further suggested transcriptional relationships among distinct stromal cell populations. This study identified SMC2, SUV39H2, and TIMELESS as candidate tissue-based molecular biomarkers for EMs and revealed alterations in stromal cell populations and immune-related features associated with the disease.
